groups.label: Approach
groups.hint: How Dim Factory should shape the plan.

options.label: Core loop first
options.hint: The smallest playable version before art and menus.
options.guidance: Plan the smallest playable loop first (start, play, score, lose or win, restart) with plain shapes, and make it fun before adding art, sound, menus or extra levels. Every step leaves the game playable.

options.label: Playtested
options.hint: Goals written as things a player can do and see.
options.guidance: Write every acceptance criterion as something a player does and sees ("Arrow keys steer the snake", "Your best score is still there after you reload"). Turn each one into a scenario in playtest.json that the test hook (?test=1) can play.

options.label: Milestones
options.hint: Stages that each end in a playable game.
options.guidance: Split the plan into a few ordered milestones (core loop, then rules and scoring, then polish and settings). Each ends in a playable game and says how to check it before the next one starts.

focus: No eval, new Function or string timers anywhere, including level editors, share codes and save loading: parse data with JSON.parse and check its shape.
Text a player types (names, level titles, messages) is shown as text (textContent), never inserted as HTML.
Saves, share codes and links are untrusted input: a broken, edited or oversized one must not crash the game or run code.
No third-party scripts, ads, analytics or trackers, and nothing loaded from a CDN: everything the game uses is in the project.
Kid-safe for a kids' game: no chat or shared free text, no outside links, ads or purchases, no flashing more than three times a second, nothing stored but local scores and settings.
No gambling or real money: no betting, loot boxes, paid random rewards or crypto.
Multiplayer: the server decides the rules and checks every move; the game in the browser is never trusted.
Personal photos stay in the project folder: the game never uploads them or sends them anywhere.
The game server binds 127.0.0.1 while you develop; listening on other addresses is a deliberate setting (HOST) for hosting it behind HTTPS.
The server checks the Origin of every WebSocket connection against an allow list and refuses the rest.
Every message is capped in size (2 KB) and rate (about 20 a second per player); bad, oversized or flooding clients get an error or are cut off, and the server never crashes.
The server is authoritative: it keeps the game state, checks every move against the rules and whose turn it is, and sends each player only what they may see.
No accounts or passwords: players meet with random, hard-to-guess room codes; rooms are capped in number and closed when empty.
The server's file handler serves only the game's public files: never server code, package files, dotfiles or paths outside the folder.

preview.note: The online game's own server. Needs a server you host to play with people elsewhere; here it runs on this computer only (127.0.0.1).

lenses.label: Comparable games
lenses.ask: Which existing games are closest to this idea, what makes them fun, and what do players praise or complain about? Name mechanics, not trademarked characters or art to copy.

lenses.label: Game feel
lenses.ask: What makes a game like this feel good to play (responsive controls, feedback, animation, sound, screen shake within reason) and which small touches matter most?

lenses.label: Smallest fun version
lenses.ask: What is the smallest version of this game that is already fun to play, and what should wait for later?

lenses.label: Controls and accessibility
lenses.ask: Which controls do players expect on a keyboard, a phone and a gamepad, and which accessibility options (remapping, pause, reduced motion, colour-blind safe palettes, no flashing) apply?

lenses.label: Difficulty curve
lenses.ask: How should difficulty start and grow in a game like this so beginners are not stuck and good players are not bored?

lenses.label: Engine choice
lenses.ask: For a small browser game like this, is plain canvas or an HTML grid enough, or does a bundled library help? Weigh size, licence and offline use.

lenses.label: Originality
lenses.ask: Which names, characters, logos and art styles in this genre are trademarked or closely tied to one game, so this game should avoid them while keeping the mechanics?

targets.label: itch.io
targets.freeTier: No upload fee for a browser game; you choose whether to charge, and what share of any sales itch.io keeps.
targets.cost: No charge to host a free game; check itch.io's current terms before you sell one.
targets.coldStarts: None: the game's files are served as they are.
targets.customDomains: The game gets a page on itch.io under your account's address.
targets.dataResidency: Served from itch.io's own servers; you cannot choose a region.

steps.label: Make a zip of the game's files, with index.html at the top of the zip
steps.note: On Windows, select the files inside the folder, right-click, then Send to and Compressed (zipped) folder. On a Mac, select them, right-click and Compress.

steps.label: Sign in to itch.io, open the menu under your name and choose Upload new project
Set Kind of project to HTML, upload the zip and tick This file will be played in the browser
Set the embed size to fit the game and turn on the fullscreen button
Save it as a draft, play it on its page, then make it public
steps.note: A draft page is visible only to you until you publish it.

targets.label: GitHub Pages
targets.freeTier: Included with GitHub's plans for public repositories, within GitHub's usage limits; private sites need a paid plan.
targets.cost: Usually no extra charge for a small public site; check the limits on size, bandwidth and builds.
targets.coldStarts: None: the files are served as they are.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with an HTTPS certificate once DNS points at GitHub.
targets.dataResidency: Served from GitHub's global network; you cannot choose a region.
targets.needs: git, and the GitHub CLI (gh) to open the repository

steps.label: Commit the workflow, then push it
In the repository settings, open Pages and set Source to GitHub Actions
steps.note: The workflow then publishes the game on every push to the branch it watches.

steps.label: Open the repository in your browser

targets.label: Netlify
targets.freeTier: A starter tier for personal projects, with monthly limits on bandwidth, build minutes and function calls.
targets.cost: Paid plans are billed per team member; usage over the limits is billed or paused, depending on the plan.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with HTTPS certificates Netlify manages.
targets.dataResidency: Static files come from a global network.
targets.needs: Node.js (the Netlify CLI runs through npx)

steps.label: Link this folder to a Netlify site
Deploy a draft to check it

targets.label: Cloudflare Pages
targets.freeTier: A starter tier with a monthly build limit and generous bandwidth for static files.
targets.cost: Paid plans add builds and features; check the current limits before you rely on them.
targets.customDomains: Supported, with HTTPS; easiest when the domain uses Cloudflare DNS.
targets.dataResidency: Served from Cloudflare's global network; regional rules need a paid plan.
targets.needs: Node.js (Wrangler, the Cloudflare CLI, runs through npx)

targets.label: Surge
targets.freeTier: A free plan for static sites on a surge.sh address, with limits. Check the provider's current pricing.
targets.cost: A paid plan adds features such as HTTPS on your own domain and password protection.
targets.customDomains: Supported: point the domain at Surge, then publish with the domain instead of the surge.sh name. HTTPS on your own domain needs the paid plan.
targets.dataResidency: Files are served from Surge's own network; there is no region to choose.
targets.needs: Node.js (the Surge CLI runs through npx)

steps.label: Build the site first if it has a build step
steps.note: The command below publishes the folder as it is: the built files, with index.html at its top.

steps.label: Publish the folder to a surge.sh address
steps.note: The first time, the Surge CLI asks for an email and a password in the terminal to make your account. If the name is taken, pick another.

steps.label: For a single-page app, answer every address with the app
steps.note: Copy index.html to 200.html in the same folder before you publish, so links to inner pages load the app.

steps.label: Use your own domain (optional)
steps.note: Point the domain at Surge as its help pages say, then run the publish command with your domain in place of the surge.sh address.

steps.label: Take it down when you no longer want it online
